headline_definitions.target_delta: DIFF_TARGET=True gives popularity(t+5) - popularity(t-5); DIFF_TARGET_PCT=True gives 100*(popularity(t+5) - popularity(t-5))/popularity(t)
headline_definitions.verified_lag_semantics: lagK[t] == y_raw[t-K] exactly (verified against released data: lag5 matches y_raw shifted 5 back on 66/66 comparable rows for BLAST; diff_lag5 == y_raw - lag5 to 7e-15)
headline_definitions.features: y_raw, reviews, research_review_diff, research_review_ratio, review_research_ratio_2, review_research_diff_2, pct_diff, y_diff, y_pct_diff, patent_count, patent_frac, patent_yearly_total, pat_div_research, lag5_pct_new, pct_diff_lag5, year_num
headline_definitions.validation: sklearn TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=30) over rows sorted by (Year, variable) - i.e. folds are contiguous year blocks shared across all topics
headline_definitions.baselines: RidgeCV on y_raw alone ('naive lag model'); RidgeCV on all numeric features ('linear model')
headline_definitions.topic_eligibility: topic must have >6 rows after filtering; rows require year_num>=1979 and Year>start (start = first 'valid' year with >=4 occurrences in the preceding 5 years)

What IS reproduced is the exact pipeline logic, evidenced by the lag baseline matching Table 1 to the last reported digit for two independent target definitions.

pct_ridge_lag_vs_paper.verdict: matches to the reported precision; resolves the delta-target definition

persistence_level.note: the no-model forecast y(t+5)=y(t) already reaches R2 0.969, so the level target is dominated by autocorrelation

pct_zero_change.note: predicting zero change on the pct target has LOWER MAE (97.56) than the paper's learned lag baseline (115.42)

leakage_positive_control.note: appending y(t+5) as a feature drives R2 to exactly 1.0, proving the harness would have detected genuine leakage

ablation_topic_block_order.note: running the same model with rows sorted by topic instead of year turns the CV into a topic-transportability test; the metric is then not a temporal estimate. The 2023 notebook's explicit sort_values(['Year','variable']) is load-bearing.

limitations: notebooks only - no package, no CLI, no test suite, no CI
no licence file: code reuse forbidden
no pinned environment: the authors' exact numbers depend on an unreconstructable stack
patent counts cannot be regenerated (PatentsView key gated, released call masked)
PubMed-by-Year is a third-party scrape with no pinned snapshot
level-target skill is dominated by persistence (R2 0.969 with no model)
leakage_risks: topic survivorship: the 125 topics were chosen in 2022 as active/notable, so backtests over 1979-2019 condition on the topic surviving into the present - the paper itself flags this
level-target illusion: popularity(t+5) ~ popularity(t), so R2 0.97+ is autocorrelation, not forecasting skill; the honest baselines are persistence (R2 0.969) and the delta target
the delta target is a 10-year span (t-5 to t+5) normalised by popularity(t); describing it as a 5-year change would overstate the horizon actually forecast
topic-level validation (paper Table 2) is the only test that removes the 'known topic' advantage, and performance drops sharply there (R2 0.86 boosting vs 0.98 temporal)
cumulative/derived features in trends_v6.csv.gz were computed once over the full history; anyone reusing the file must not treat per-row values as point-in-time known

decision.scope: method-level reimplementation only (popularity normalisation + review:research ratio + temporal validation protocol); zero code reuse
decision.reason: the reproduction is strong enough to trust the method (lag baseline matches Table 1 exactly for two target definitions), and MedRadar already has a documented weak publication path that these two transforms directly improve; but the absence of any licence forbids reusing code or data files, so only an independent implementation with attribution is permissible
